pairs.subject: quality-gates
pairs.evidence: src/lib/github/governance.ts:96 The ingestion reduces the ruleset's required-status-checks rule to a boolean and drops the list of required check names. No downstream reader can then diff the checks the merge decision requires against the checks the pipeline emits, so a rule requiring a renamed or never-emitted check (a requirement nothing satisfies) is credited as enforcement. passport.ts:361 derives `enforced` from this boolean, and governance.test.ts:75 credits a rule that names no check.

techniques.evidence: src/lib/github/governance.ts:96 The binding is read only as 'a rule exists'. The required check names (parameters.required_status_checks) are discarded, so the required-vs-emitted inventory the technique demands cannot be computed, and a requirement that matches nothing reads as enforced.

src/lib/github/governance.ts:80 An unreadable rulesets response becomes governance UNKNOWN (null), never 'zero active rules'. A hole in the instrument therefore cannot read as a measured 'no protection' (or as compliance) to the downstream gate.

src/lib/github/codeowners.ts:24 CODEOWNERS is resolved in GitHub's own precedence order (the engine's resolution), not by the first file in the fetch array, so a stale lower-precedence copy is never read as the effective one.

pairs.registryProposal: enforcement-binding is written for a repo auditing its own merge binding. A conformance scanner that ingests other repos' bindings meets the same failure one level up: flattening the required-check list to 'required: yes' at ingestion makes the rename failure undetectable for every consumer. The technique could say that a binding read for assessment must keep the required check names so the inventory diff stays possible.
